"Northern Territory police were found guilty of systemic negligence after failing to prevent the death of 23-year-old Dale Scott Walkinshaw, who died in the back of a caged police vehicle last year despite repeated warnings about suicide risks in custody vans, a coronial inquest has revealed. Coroner Greg Cavanagh condemned the NT Police for disregarding a 2013 internal report that urged the installation of CCTV cameras in all caged vehicles following a prior death in custody—a recommendation left unaddressed for over a decade. 'The lack of action was not an oversight but a choice,' Cavanagh stated in his findings, emphasizing that between 2013 and Walkinshaw’s death, at least 16 suicide attempts had occurred in police vans, with six individuals only discovered once they were semi-conscious or dead. 'It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when,' he added, his words underscoring a pattern of preventable tragedy.  

The inquest centered on the evening of September 16, 2023, when officers responding to a noise complaint near Darwin Airport stumbled upon the aftermath of a violent collision. A Toyota Hilux lay crumpled against a palm tree at the intersection of Stuart Highway and Bargot Road, its passenger—a young woman Walkinshaw had met hours earlier at a bar—suffering a severe spinal injury. Walkinshaw, blood alcohol level at 0.149, hid behind nearby shrubs before surrendering to police. Described in court documents as 'vulnerable' due to a history of mental health struggles, he was placed in the rear compartment of a patrol vehicle without surveillance. Unseen by officers, he attempted to take his own life during transit. By the time he was discovered, it was too late.  

Cavanagh’s report detailed how the 2013 recommendation for CCTV had been explicitly linked to reducing custodial deaths, yet NT Police leadership dismissed it as 'unnecessary' and 'cost-prohibitive.' Meanwhile, internal logs revealed officers had documented self-harm incidents in custody vans nearly monthly, with detainees using seat belts, clothing, or restraints to inflict harm. In one 2019 case, a man strangled himself with his own shirt sleeve; in another, a teenager was found unconscious after slamming his head against the cage divider. 'Each of these was a warning,' Cavanagh said. 'Each was ignored.'  

Walkinshaw’s family wept as the coroner described the final moments: officers, unaware of his distress, continued their route to the station. His death—which his mother called 'a murder by apathy'—has reignited calls for accountability in a jurisdiction with Australia’s highest rate of Indigenous incarceration and custodial deaths. Advocacy groups now demand mandatory welfare checks, real-time monitoring, and cultural safety training for officers. Yet NT Police Minister Natasha Fyles offered only a tepid acknowledgment, stating, 'Lessons will be learned,' while refusing to commit to CCTV installation.  

As dusk fell on Darwin the day of the ruling, a makeshift shrine of flowers and handwritten notes grew outside the coroner’s court—a silent rebuke to a system that knew exactly how to prevent these deaths but chose not to act."

"Northern Territory police were found guilty of systemic negligence after failing to prevent the death of 23-year-old Dale Scott Walkinshaw, who died in the back of a caged police vehicle last year despite repeated warnings about suicide risks in custody vans, a coronial inquest has revealed. 'The lack of action was not an oversight but a choice,' Cavanagh stated in his findings, emphasizing that between 2013 and Walkinshaw’s death, at least 16 suicide attempts had occurred in police vans, with six individuals only discovered once they were semi-conscious or dead. 'It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when,' he added, his words underscoring a pattern of preventable tragedy.  

The inquest centered on the evening of September 16, 2023, when officers responding to a noise complaint near Darwin Airport stumbled upon the aftermath of a violent collision. A Toyota Hilux lay crumpled against a palm tree at the intersection of Stuart Highway and Bargot Road, its passenger—a young woman Walkinshaw had met hours earlier at a bar—suffering a severe spinal injury. Walkinshaw, blood alcohol level at 0.149, hid behind nearby shrubs before surrendering to police. Described in court documents as 'vulnerable' due to a history of mental health struggles, he was placed in the rear compartment of a patrol vehicle without surveillance. Unseen by officers, he attempted to take his own life during transit. By the time he was discovered, it was too late.  

Cavanagh’s report detailed how the 2013 recommendation for CCTV had been explicitly linked to reducing custodial deaths, yet NT Police leadership dismissed it as 'unnecessary' and 'cost-prohibitive.' Meanwhile, internal logs revealed officers had documented self-harm incidents in custody vans nearly monthly, with detainees using seat belts, clothing, or restraints to inflict harm. In one 2019 case, a man strangled himself with his own shirt sleeve; in another, a teenager was found unconscious after slamming his head against the cage divider. 'Each of these was a warning,' Cavanagh said. 'Each was ignored.'  

Walkinshaw’s family wept as the coroner described the final moments: officers, unaware of his distress, continued their route to the station. His death—which his mother called 'a murder by apathy'—has reignited calls for accountability in a jurisdiction with Australia’s highest rate of Indigenous incarceration and custodial deaths. Advocacy groups now demand mandatory welfare checks, real-time monitoring, and cultural safety training for officers. Yet NT Police Minister Natasha Fyles offered only a tepid acknowledgment, stating, 'Lessons will be learned,' while refusing to commit to CCTV installation.
